paper_title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: https://fr0zencrane.github.io/project-glyphatlas/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Scene text synthesis aims to render accurate, legible text in specified regions of scene image while keeping it visually coherent with its surroundings [13, 36], supporting applications such as photo editing [3, 38] and poster design [8]. To achieve this, the conditioning strategy in this area usually prerenders the target text at its intended locations into glyph image, which jointly specifies layout and glyph structure for diffusion model [13, 35, 36, 40, 41]. This representation is widely adopted because it is spatially aligned with the scene while specifying glyph structure: the model knows exactly which glyph to generate and where each glyph belongs. However, this spatial alignment also ties the resolution of each glyph reference to its target region size, leaving small, dense and structure-complex text with limited pixels to represent its strokes [40]. The model is therefore misled by the flawed stroke cues in the glyph image, yielding incomplete, merged, or distorted characters. We argue that such failures arise because the glyph image is overloaded with two roles. As spatial anchor, it works well, since it consistently conveys where each glyph belongs and roughly what it looks like regardless of region size. As stroke reference, however, it degrades with region size. Prior work has sought to compensate or replace with 1 glyph embeddings extracted by OCR or other visual text encoders [19, 35, 48], but the remedy has three drawbacks. It introduces an additional encoder, its recognition-oriented features are trained to be invariant to exactly the strokelevel variation that needs to be rendered, and once injected as global tokens the embeddings lose their correspondence with the region they describe. In light of the above, we propose GlyphAtlas, which decouples the two roles while keeping them collaborative. The glyph image is retained solely for layout and coarse glyph structure, while fine-grained stroke guidance is supplied by dedicated glyph atlas. Specifically, the proposed glyph atlas renders each character or word in separate cell at resolution independent of its target region, so that every text region gains access to detailed stroke reference even when its scene-aligned glyph occupies only few pixels. Crucially, atlas cells are encoded with the diffusion backbones native VAE rather than dedicated text encoder. Benefiting from the VAEs pixel-level reconstruction objective, its features preserve low-level stroke structure and remain sensitive to stroke variation, providing detail-rich guidance without introducing any auxiliary encoder. To bind the atlas back to the layout, we introduce atlasanchored attention, where scene and glyph-image tokens retrieve stroke detail only from the atlas cells assigned to the text regions they overlap, while each cell attends to the prompt and its own region. Local stroke evidence thus refines both the scene features and their glyph condition without ever losing regional correspondence. The resulting coarse-tofine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering, as the model no longer has to recover fine structure from an under-resolved condition but only to refine coarse structure already placed in the scene. GlyphAtlas is trained with mask-weighted flow matching objective [15, 18] and timestep-weighted text perceptual loss, which together target writing accuracy and background consistency. Since the atlas grows with the number of characters, we further apply random resolution augmentation to atlas cells during training, which lets the atlas token budget be reduced at inference to accommodate scenes with many text regions. We evaluate GlyphAtlas on standard benchmarks and in the settings that strain glyph-image conditioning. GlyphAtlas achieves the highest sentence accuracy among compared methods on AnyText-benchmark [36], TextOCR [31], Total-Text [5], and ReCTS [17]. On unseen scripts in STIPLAR [29], it leads all methods without language-specific fine-tuning by large margins. Ablations trace these gains to the glyph atlas, which improves sentence accuracy by 9.6 points on small Total-Text regions, 8.1 points on Chinese text, and over 20 points on Korean and Arabic over an identically trained glyph-image-only model. Our main contributions are as follows: We identify that glyph-image conditioning conflates two roles: it remains reliable spatial anchor, yet degrades as stroke reference once regions shrink. We propose GlyphAtlas, which decouples yet coordinates the two roles: the glyph atlas supplies region-independent stroke references, and atlas-anchored attention binds them back to the regions laid out by the glyph image. GlyphAtlas achieves state-of-the-art performance on four scene text benchmarks, and ablations attribute the gains on small, dense, structurally complex, and unseen-script text to the glyph atlas together with atlas-anchored attention.

sections.title: 2.1 Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
sections.content: Diffusion models [11, 28] are the dominant paradigm for visual generation, evolving from UNet-based latent diffusion [25, 28] to diffusion transformers (DiTs) [24] trained with flow matching [15, 18], as represented by SD3 [7] and FLUX [1]. Conditioned on text prompt alone, these models offer weak control over spatial layout, and visual text exposes this most clearly, since word must appear at specific place with specific spelling [16]. The common remedy is an additional image condition, injected through an auxiliary branch in UNets [45] or concatenated with the noisy latent into unified sequence in DiTs [2, 34, 47]. Scene text synthesis is an instance of this setup in which the condition is usually pre-rendered glyph image, and we detail in Sec. 2.2 how this condition is built and where it falls short.

sections.title: 2.2 Scene Text Synthesis
sections.content: Scene text synthesis covers scene text generation and editing, both of which render legible text in specified regions of scene image [13, 36]. Early methods composite rendered text onto natural images [9] or edit existing text with GANs [38]. Diffusion models have since become dominant, first as UNet-based inpainting models with auxiliary glyph conditions [3, 4, 12, 36, 41] and recently as fine-tuned DiTs [13, 40]. Across these models, the prevailing condition is glyph image: the target text pre-rendered in canonical font at its target locations on scene-sized canvas [13, 36, 40, 41]. Being pixel-aligned with the scene, one glyph image serves as both spatial anchor and stroke reference, but each glyph then receives only as many pixels as its region allows, so small, dense, and structure-complex text remains commonly failure [8, 40]. region-independent reference lifts this limit but gives up the alignment, which existing work restores along two routes. The first injects glyph embeddings from OCR recognizers or glyph-aligned text encoders [8, 19, 35, 48]. This requires an additional encoder whose character set bounds its coverage [35], yields recognition features invariant to the very stroke variation to be 2 rendered, and, unless routed region-wise [19], detaches each embedding from the region it describes [35]. The second, closer to ours, renders each text item as separate glyph patch and binds it to its region through positional encodings [22, 39] or attention masks [30]. Developed mainly for text-to-image rendering, these methods replace the glyph image rather than complement it, so no coarse structure is placed in the scene to be refined, and text is missed or corrupted once the binding becomes ambiguous [22, 39]. it keeps the GlyphAtlas takes neither route exclusively: glyph image as spatial anchor and coarse structure, and adds glyph atlas of VAE-encoded cells, bound region-wise by atlas-anchored attention, solely to refine it.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Fig. 2 presents an overview of GlyphAtlas. It conditions diffusion transformer on two complementary glyph references: the glyph image, which anchors the layout and coarse glyph structure, and the proposed glyph atlas, which supplies fine-grained stroke references and is bound to the layout by atlas-anchored attention. In the following, we first present the task, the flow matching formulation, and the backbone in Sec. 3.1, then introduce the glyph atlas and atlas-anchored attention in Sec. 3.2, and finally describe the training objectives and atlas budgeting in Sec. 3.3.

sections.title: 3.3 Optimization and Atlas Budgeting
sections.content: Training follows the masked reconstruction setting common in diffusion-based scene text synthesis [3, 13, 36], where the target is the scene image itself, so z0 in Eq. (2) is its latent, and the model learns to re-synthesize the text inside from Imask, , G, A, and p. All DiT weights are updated together with the atlas projection and embeddings, while the VAE and the text encoders stay frozen. Two objectives steer 5 where the mean is taken over all latent elements. Text regions thus receive twice the weight of the background, which emphasizes text accuracy without discarding the background term that preserves scene consistency. Timestep-weighted text perceptual loss. Flow matching supervises latents and is agnostic to legibility, so we add pixel-space loss on the text. Since z0 = ϵ by Eq. (2), the prediction vθ yields one-step estimate ˆz0 = ϵ vθ of the clean latent, which we decode into = D(ˆz0) with the frozen VAE decoder. We crop every text region from and and feed the crops to frozen text recognizer [14]. Following AnyText [36], the text perceptual loss LOCR is the mean squared difference between the recognizer features of corresponding crops, averaged over valid crops and set to zero when none exists. The full objective is = Lflow + 2t α LOCR, (7) with α = 0.25. Since E[t] = 1/2 under logit-normal sampling, the factor 2t has unit expectation and α keeps its meaning as the average weight, while supervision shifts toward high-noise inputs, where the structure of the glyphs is decided. Gradients flow through the frozen decoder and recognizer into the DiT. Atlas Budgeting. The atlas grows linearly with the number of units, and each cell costs tokens in proportion to its area. Since cell resolution is decoupled from region size, it trades stroke detail against sequence length, which lets scenes with many text regions fit fixed token budget. To make the model robust to this trade-off, we add second training stage after training at cell height of 64 pixels, in which each non-punctuation unit is re-rendered at 48, 64, or 80 pixels with probabilities 0.2, 0.7, and 0.1, while punctuation stays at 64 pixels. Consequently, during inference, the user can either set one cell height for all units or specifies total token budget, which heuristic allocator distributes across cells, giving smaller scene glyphs higher resolution. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We describe the experimental setup in Sec. 4.1, compare GlyphAtlas with state-of-the-art methods in Sec. 4.2, and present ablation studies and analysis in Sec. 4.3.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. GlyphAtlas is trained on 1.54M images, consisting of 1.46M images from AnyWord-3M [36] and 75.6K real-scene images from the training splits of CTW [43], TextOCR [31], HierText [20], ReCTS [17], LSVT [33], MLT2019 [23], Total-Text [5], and STIPLAR [29], after annotation filtering, duplicate removal, and resolution normalization. For ablations and zero-shot multilingual evaluation, we additionally train GlyphAtlas-Bi on balanced 100K ChineseEnglish subset that contains no other script. Dataset construction details are provided in the supplement. Benchmarks. We evaluate in three settings. (i) Scene text generation on AnyText-benchmark [36], with 1,000 English and 1,000 Chinese images containing 4,181 and (ii) Scene text editing on the Tex2,092 text lines. tOCR [31], Total-Text [5], and ReCTS [17] test sets released with TextFlux [40], with 3,112/265/1,622 images and 19,531/1,241/4,858 text regions. On Total-Text we further report three overlapping subsets that strain glyph-image conditioning, namely curved text, small text whose short side is below 16 pixels, and cluttered images with six or more text regions. (iii) Zero-shot scene text editing in unseen scripts on STIPLAR [29], with 385 Japanese, 2,079 Korean, and 981 Arabic examples. GlyphAtlas is evaluated in (i) and (ii), and GlyphAtlas-Bi in (iii). Metrics. Following AnyText [36], text accuracy is measured by sentence accuracy (ACC) and normalized edit distance (NED) of an OCR model on the generated text regions, and visual quality by FID [10] and LPIPS [46] against the reference images. On STIPLAR, metrics are computed on the edited text crops with language-specific recognizers, and NED and LPIPS are reported in the supplement. Baselines. We compare GlyphAtlas with AnyText [36], AnyText2 [35], DreamText [37], TextSSR [42], FLUX-Text [13], TextFlux [40], and STELLAR [29] using their official checkpoints and sampling settings, and take the results of earlier methods in Tab. 1 from their papers. The closest regionindependent conditioning methods cannot be run under our editing protocol, as EasyText [22] and GlyphPrinter [30] release only prompt-and-layout generation without source scene or mask, and GlyphAnchor [39] has no public code. Implementation details. GlyphAtlas is built on FLUX.1Fill-dev [1] and trained as described in Sec. 3.3 with AdamW [21], weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping 0.5. It is trained for 5 epochs (about 60K updates) with global batch size of 128 on 32 H200 GPUs, where the learning rate decays from 5 105 to 1 105 with cosine schedule in the first epoch and stays constant afterwards. Atlas cells are rendered at 64 pixels in the first epoch and with random resolution augmentation in the remaining four. GlyphAtlasBi and all ablation models are trained for 12.5K iterations with batch size of 8 on eight H200 GPUs with constant learning rate of 2 105 after warm-up, with atlas cells fixed at 64 pixels unless stated otherwise. All results are sampled with 10 Euler steps and guidance scale of 1.0.

sections.content: ods Scene text generation. Tab. 1 presents the results on AnyText-benchmark. GlyphAtlas achieves the best ACC, NED, and FID in both languages, surpassing FLUX-Text, the strongest baseline, by 4.5 ACC points in English and 6.6 in Chinese, with English LPIPS slightly behind FLUX-Text. The gain is larger in Chinese, whose characters carry the most complex stroke structure, which agrees with our analysis in Sec. 1 as the propose atlas contributes the most where the glyph image provides the weakest stroke reference. Scene text editing. Tab. 2 presents the results on three realscene benchmarks, where text regions are small, irregular, and numerous, with 6.3 regions per image on TextOCR. GlyphAtlas achieves the best ACC and NED on all three benchmarks, exceeding the best baseline by 5.4, 9.1, and 19.0 ACC points on TextOCR, Total-Text, and ReCTS, with FID comparable to FLUX-Text and TextFlux. The gain peaks on ReCTS, which pairs Chinese characters with the small regions of real scenes, the two conditions under which the glyph image is the most under-resolved. Zero-shot editing in unseen scripts. Tab. 3 presents the results on STIPLAR with GlyphAtlas-Bi, whose training data contain no Korean or Arabic. Among methods without language-specific training, GlyphAtlas-Bi is the most accurate in all three scripts, exceeding the best such baseline by 19.7, 33.1, and 33.1 ACC points. It also surpasses STELLAR in Japanese, while STELLAR stays ahead in Korean and Arabic with separate model fine-tuned on each language. Notably, FLUX-Text and TextFlux share the backbone with GlyphAtlas-Bi and are trained on far more data, so the gap stems from the glyph reference rather than the backbone or the data, which we verify in Sec. 4.3. Qualitative results. Fig. 4 compares GlyphAtlas with AnyText2, TextFlux, and FLUX-Text on the four benchmarks. The baselines misspell or garble text in every row, such as GOON$ on the album cover, where the dollar sign is copied from the DIBIA$E header, 16 and 18 for the 10 and 12 on the watch bezel, 1990 and 1900 on the round sign, and wrong or missing characters in the small menu line of the shop sign, whereas GlyphAtlas renders these targets correctly and keeps the hand-drawn outlines, the engraved bezel, and the raised letters of their carriers.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies and Analysis
sections.content: All models in this section follow the recipe of GlyphAtlas-Bi in Sec. 4.1 and differ from it in one factor at time. We ablate the glyph reference, locate the source of zero-shot transfer, and examine the atlas budget. Glyph references. The first two rows of Tab. 4 use single reference and verify that the two are complementary. The glyph image leads on English and curved text by 3.6 and 2.5 ACC points, where layout is the main difficulty and Latin strokes survive scene-resolution rendering. While the atlas leads on Chinese and small text by 6.4 and 4.8 points and on all three STIPLAR scripts, where the glyph image is under-resolved. This split matches the two roles identified in Sec. 1, and combining the two in the last row inherits the strength of both, improving on the glyph image alone by 2.0 points in English, 8.1 in Chinese, 9.6 on small text, and 7.6 on cluttered images. Atlas-anchored attention. The last two rows hold both references fixed and replace atlas-anchored attention with full attention, which lets every token attend to every cell. Anchoring improves ACC on every Total-Text subset, most on small text (21.69 vs. 27.21) and cluttered images (52.12 vs. 56.08), and by 6.6 points in Arabic. These are the cases where glyphs are tiny and cells of several regions coexist, so region under full attention can draw strokes from the cells of its neighbors, which is the interference the mask in Eq. (5) removes. The same effect explains the large margin of GlyphAtlas on TextOCR in Tab. 2, whose images carry the most regions. The one exception is Japanese, where full attention leads by 3.4 points. Source of zero-shot transfer. The four models share the recipe, so what they know about Korean and Arabic comes either from the pretrained prior or from the glyph reference at test time. The glyph image alone reaches 37.90 and 19.27 ACC, the most the prior recovers from scene-resolution rendering, whereas the atlas alone reaches 58.25 and 39.96, and the combination 66.96 and 39.55. As anticipated, the transfer comes from the atlas, whose cells present the strokes of an unseen glyph at resolution the model can copy, which the VAE encodes without script-specific vocabulary and atlas-anchored attention delivers to the right region. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose GlyphAtlas, scene text synthesis framework, to address the challenge of rendering stroke-accurate text when the glyph image is under-resolved for small, dense, or structurally complex text. We first introduce the glyph atlas, which renders each character or word in separate cell at resolution independent of its target region and supplies fine-grained stroke references. Building on this, we design atlas-anchored attention to bind each atlas cell to its own text region, so that the glyph image anchors the layout while the atlas refines the strokes. In addition, random resolution augmentation of atlas cells makes the atlas token budget adjustable at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas outperforms existing methods in text accuracy on four scene text benchmarks and transfers zero-shot to scripts unseen in training, demonstrating significant potential in scene text synthesis for low-resource languages. 8 Limitation. Although GlyphAtlas achieves high text accuracy, its atlas cells are rendered in uniform font and thus specify strokes rather than typography, leaving occasional errors in font weight and color. Also, the appended atlas tokens inevitably incurs extra inference cost over glyph-image-only conditioning despite the introduced adjustable budget. We regard these as promising directions for future works.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: This supplement is organized as follows. Sec. details the experimental setup: the construction of the training data, the evaluation protocol, and the implementation of GlyphAtlas and of the compared methods. Sec. extends the related work of the main paper. Secs. CE report the full results behind the abbreviated tables of the main paper: the comparison with state-of-the-art methods (Sec. C), the ablation studies together with two further design ablations (Sec. D), and the atlas budget study with its inference cost (Sec. E). Sec. closes with more qualitative results on scene text generation, scene text editing, and out-of-distribution case studies. Unless stated otherwise, every ablation model follows the recipe of GlyphAtlas-Bi in Sec. 4.1 of the main paper and differs from it in one factor at time, and ACC denotes sentence accuracy on AnyText-benchmark.

sections.title: A Experimental Setup
sections.content: We describe how the training data are built (Sec. A.1), how every reported number is computed (Sec. A.2), and how GlyphAtlas and the compared methods are implemented and run (Sec. A.3). A.1 Dataset Construction GlyphAtlas is trained on pool of 1.54M real-scene images, and GlyphAtlas-Bi and all ablations on balanced 100K ChineseEnglish subset. We describe how each is built. Main training pool. The pool combines 1.46M images from the deduplicated AnyWord-3M [36] with 75.6K additional real-scene images drawn from the training splits of CTW [43], TextOCR [31], HierText [20], ReCTS [17], LSVT [33], MLT2019 [23], Total-Text [5], and STIPLAR [29]. For the additional images, we take at most two 512 512 crops per source image, at the original scale and, optionally, with up to 2 enlargement, and never resize crop after cropping. region is kept only if its smallest character is at least 20 pixels, its local contrast and sharpness pass fixed thresholds, and it overlaps an ignore region by at most 5%. Pixel-level duplicates are matched against AnyWord-3M and resolved in its favor. Original transcriptions are retained throughout. Bilingual subset. The subset used for GlyphAtlas-Bi and the ablations contains 50K Chinese-annotated and 50K Latinonly images, selected deterministically from the pool so that the choice is reproducible and contains no script other than Chinese and Latin. It thus isolates the effect of each design factor from the long multilingual tail of the full pool, and leaves Japanese, Korean, and Arabic entirely unseen for the zero-shot evaluation of Sec. 4.2 of the main paper. A.2 Evaluation Protocol Text accuracy. On AnyText-benchmark we score the generated regions with the ModelScope DuGuang recognizer [14], following the AnyText protocol [36]; the PPOCRv3 recognizer that serves as the training perceptual teacher is used only as diagnostic and never produces reported accuracy. region is cropped from the output with its annotated polygon, rotated upright when its height exceeds 1.2 its width, resized to height of 48 pixels with width capped at 320, and padded to width 320. Sentence accuracy (ACC) is the fraction of regions whose recognized string equals the target exactly, averaged over all scored regions rather than over images, with no case folding or punctuation stripping. Normalized edit distance is NED = 1 Lev(ˆy, y)/ max(ˆy, y), higher being better, averaged over the same regions. On STIPLAR we use the language-specific PP-OCRv4 recognizers for Japanese, Korean, and Arabic, each run on the edited crop; for Arabic we keep the logical character order and additionally remove spaces, matching the STELLAR evaluation [29]. ACC is recognizer-dependent estimate of legibility, not per-stroke guarantee. Image quality. FID [10] uses the 2,048-dimensional Inception features and LPIPS [46] the AlexNet features. On AnyText-benchmark and the real-scene editing benchmarks both are computed on the full images; on STIPLAR, where only crop is edited, both are computed on the edited crops, with LPIPS inputs resized to 256 256. Total-Text subsets. The three Total-Text subsets reported in the main paper are defined on the TextFlux-released view of 265 images with 1,241 edited regions. Curved collects the regions annotated as curved; small collects the regions whose short side is below 16 pixels on the 512 512 canvas; cluttered collects the regions of images with six or more edited regions. The subsets overlap, and region is scored under every subset it satisfies. A.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We complement the implementation details of Sec. 4.1 of the main paper with the components that are not specified there. 12 Glyph image and prompt. Following FLUX-Text [13], each target string is drawn into the glyph image in Arial Unicode, centered in the minimum-area rectangle of its region and rotated with it. Its font size is 0.8 of the rectangles short side, reduced when the string would overflow the long side, and spaces are inserted between characters to spread short string along the rectangle, after which the glyph image is binarized. The atlas cells are rendered in the same font. During training, the prompt is the image caption followed by one of ten template phrases and the target strings, e.g., bookstore, that reads BOOKS ., and at most eight text regions are used per image. Glyph atlas. Text units are formed by deterministic rule: each Han character is unit, each word of letter-based script such as Latin or Arabic is word unit, with digits, internal apostrophes, and hyphens kept inside it, combining marks stay with their base character, and spaces produce no cell. Japanese kana and Korean syllables are character units. character is rendered white on black into 56 56 box centered in 64 64 cell. word is rendered at an ink height of at most 56 pixels into strip whose width is the smallest multiple of 64 pixels exceeding the ink width by at least 8 pixels, and the strip is split into 64 64 tiles that all belong to the same unit. Each tile is encoded with the posterior mean of the frozen VAE, normalized with the shift and scale of the VAE, and packed into 2 2 latent patches, which gives 16 tokens of dimension 64. cell of height and width thus costs hw/256 tokens, i.e., 9, 16, and 25 tokens for square cell at 48, 64, and 80 pixels, and cells at other heights are re-rendered from the font outlines rather than resized from 64-pixel bitmap. Atlas tokens and attention. Atlas tokens are projected to the model width of 3,072 by bias-free linear layer initialized as described in Sec. 3.2 of the main paper. two-layer MLP, whose output layer is initialized to zero, adds an embedding of the position of each token inside its cell together with the normalized unit index and the number of units in its region. These two modules are the only new parameters, 0.59M in total against 11.9B in the backbone. Atlas tokens are appended to the glyph-image tokens and share their modulation, and their rotary positions place each region in its own band of rows on canvas separate from the scene grid, with the cells of region in reading order. Atlas-anchored attention is computed without dense mask. Queries are grouped by the set of regions that their patch overlaps, where 16 16-pixel patch overlaps region if any of its pixels lies inside the region, and each group runs standard scaled dot-product attention over the keys that Eq. (5) of the main paper allows it. Training. We use AdamW [21] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and ϵ = 108, keep the master weights and optimizer states in FP32 with BF16 computation, and shard the model with FSDP. Every GPU processes one image per step; for GlyphAtlas, gradients are accumulated over four steps on the 32 GPUs to reach the global batch size of 128. The prompt and the glyph image are each dropped with probability 0.1, and the atlas is dropped whenever the glyph image is. For LOCR, each region is cropped from and along the minimum bounding rectangle of its mask, resized and padded to the 48 320 input of the frozen PP-OCRv3 recognizer [14], and compared through the features that the recognizer feeds to its CTC classifier. The reference branch runs without gradients, and no crop is filtered by its transcription or by the recognizers confidence. Inference. All benchmark images are generated at 512 512 with 10 Euler steps, guidance scale of 1.0, seed 42, and BF16, with 64-pixel cells unless stated otherwise. Compared methods. For the results we measure, each compared method runs from its official checkpoint with its recommended sampling: AnyText [36] with 20 steps and guidance 9, AnyText2 [35] with 20 steps and guidance 7.5, FLUX-Text [13] with 28 steps and guidance 3.5, and TextFlux [40] with 50 steps and guidance 30. TextSSR [42] edits the regions of an image one after another with its native 20-step local editor, and on STIPLAR it uses its released font for Japanese and Arial Unicode MS for Korean and Arabic. DreamText [37] accepts only ASCII targets, so its results in Tabs. 1 and 2 of the main paper are computed, with 50 steps and guidance 5, on the images it supports: 950 English and 91 Chinese images of AnyText-benchmark and 2,539, 254, and 75 images of TextOCR, Total-Text, and ReCTS. STELLAR [29] uses its released stage-2 model for each language with 50 inversion and 50 editing steps at guidance 2, on its native 256 256 text crops. On STIPLAR, GlyphAtlas, AnyText2, FLUX-Text, and TextFlux receive square scene crop centered on the source text box, whose side is four times the longer side of the box, clamped to 2561,024 pixels, and resized to 512 512; TextFlux stacks its glyph canvas above this crop into 512 1024 input.

sections.content: B.1 Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Diffusion models [11, 28] have become the dominant paradigm for visual generation. Conditioned on text prompt alone, these models offer weak control over spatial layout and over exact symbol identity, and visual text exposes both weaknesses at once, since word must appear at specific place with specific spelling [16]. The common remedy is an additional image condition that states what the prompt cannot. In UNet-based models it is injected through an auxiliary branch [45]; in DiTs it is encoded by the same VAE as the image and concatenated with the noisy latent into unified token sequence, so that the two interact through ordinary self-attention [2, 34, 47]. The latter design is relevant to us for two reasons: the condition needs no dedicated encoder, and an attention mask can restrict which condition tokens each image token sees. Scene text synthesis follows this recipe with pre-rendered glyph image as the condition, and Sec. B.2 discusses how this condition is built and where it falls short. B.2 Scene Text Synthesis Scene text synthesis covers scene text generation and editing, both rendering legible text in specified regions of scene image while keeping it coherent with the surroundings [13, 36]. Early methods composite rendered text onto natural images for data synthesis [9] or edit existing text with GANs by transferring the style of the source text to the target string [38]. Diffusion models have since taken over. UNet-based methods formulate the task as inpainting and add auxiliary glyph conditions, such as character-level 14 segmentation masks [4], glyph images fed through control branch [36, 41], or glyph features from text or OCR encoder [3, 12]. Recent methods fine-tune DiTs instead, either with the glyph image as an extra input channel [13] or by concatenating it spatially with the scene so that the backbone copies glyphs through in-context attention [40]. Across these models, the prevailing condition is glyph image, where the target text is pre-rendered in canonical font at its target locations on scene-sized canvas [13, 36, 40, 41]. Its appeal is that one image, pixel-aligned with the scene, serves as both spatial anchor and stroke reference: the model knows where each glyph belongs and roughly what it looks like. Its cost is that scene-aligned reference inherits the scenes per-region resolution, so each glyph receives as many pixels as its region allows rather than as its strokes require. Small, dense, and structurally complex text is accordingly the commonly reported failure case, with the glyph image itself identified as the cause [8, 40]. This is the dilemma of the area: scenealigned reference anchors well but describes strokes poorly, while region-independent reference describes strokes well but must be bound back to the scene. Existing work restores the binding along two routes. The first route injects glyph embeddings from OCR recognizers or glyph-aligned text encoders, either in place of the glyph image or alongside it [8, 19, 35, 36, 48]. Embeddings are compact and independent of region size, but they have three drawbacks that mirror the issues raised in Sec. 1 of the main paper. They require an additional encoder whose character set bounds the glyphs it can describe, so unseen characters are poorly covered [35]. Their features are trained for recognition, which rewards invariance to exactly the stroke-level variation that rendering must reproduce. And once injected as prompt tokens they lose correspondence with the region they describe, which is why later work adds position encoders [8, 35] or region-wise cross-attention [19] to restore it. The second route, closer to ours, renders each text item as separate glyph patch at fixed font size and binds the patch to its region through positional encodings remapped into the target grid [22, 39] or through an attention mask that pairs each patch with its region [30]. These methods are developed mainly for text-to-image rendering, where the whole image is synthesized from prompt and box layout, and they replace the glyph image rather than complement it. Layout is thus carried only by indices or masks, no coarse structure is placed in the scene to be refined, and text is missed or corrupted once the binding becomes ambiguous, as when regions overlap or anchoring is removed [22, 39]. GlyphAtlas takes neither route exclusively. It keeps the glyph image as spatial anchor and coarse structure, and adds glyph atlas of cells encoded by the backbones own VAE, bound region-wise by atlas-anchored attention, solely to refine that structure. All rows use the mask-weighted flow matching loss Lflow and differ in the pixel-space text supervision added to it: none, the feature-based perceptual loss of FLUXText [13] built on ODM [6], or our recognizer-based LOCR, at fixed weight or with the timestep weight 2t. These results demonstrate that: 1) pixel-space text supervision remains indispensable alongside the atlas, as removing it drops ACC to 70.08 and 62.19, 15.8 and 13.8 points below GlyphAtlas-Bi; 2) the recognizer-based LOCR is the more effective supervision, as at fixed weight of 0.25 it reaches 84.79 and 75.62 against the best ODM setting at 83.30 and 70.27, gain of 1.5 and 5.4 points, largest in Chinese, whose characters differ in exactly the stroke-level detail that recognizer features separate; 3) larger fixed weight trades image quality for accuracy, as raising from 0.25 to 1.0 adds at most 1.4 ACC points in English and 1.0 in Chinese while FID rises by 1.0 and 1.7; 4) the timestep weight 2t obtains this accuracy at lower cost in image quality, as 0.25 2t improves on the fixed 0.25 by 1.1 and 0.4 ACC points at nearly unchanged FID and LPIPS, and comes within 0.3 and 0.6 points of the most accurate fixed weights at an FID 0.9 and 1.5 lower than that of = 1.0, confirming the premise of Sec. 3.3 of the main paper that glyph structure is decided at high-noise timesteps. We therefore set α = 0.25 with the timestep weight. The FID and LPIPS that LOCR costs relative to ODM is the trade-off behind the LPIPS gap to FLUX-Text, which uses the ODM loss, in Tab. 1 of the main paper. character cell costs tokens in proportion to its area: 9, 16, and 25 tokens at heights 48, 64, and 80 pixels, so the atlas grows linearly with the number of text units and with cell resolution. This section specifies the token allocator used at inference, reports the full traintest grid of cell heights, gives the complete results behind the atlas budget paragraph in Sec. 4.3 of the main paper, and records the inference cost. Token allocator. The allocator is designed for efficient inference: it fits the atlas to target budget of tokens and, within that budget, raises the resolution of the cells that need clear stroke detail as far as possible. cell needs detail most when its glyph is small in the glyph image, which then underresolves its strokes, and least when the glyph is already large there. The allocator therefore ranks the cells by the size of their glyph in the glyph image, measured as the short side of its rendered strokes, and proceeds in three passes. First, every cell starts at 64 pixels, and any cell whose glyph is already at least 80 pixels in the glyph image is lowered to 48, as the atlas adds little where the glyph image is well resolved. Second, if the total still exceeds , cells are lowered from 64 to 48 pixels in order of decreasing glyph size until it fits. Third, the remaining budget promotes the smallest glyphs first, from 48 to 80 and then to 64 pixels, as far as allows. Punctuation stays at 64 pixels throughout. Every text unit is kept, so the budget is soft: under 512-token budget, two of the 1,000 Chinese images still exceed it, the longest at 794 tokens. Cell resolution. Tab. S5 trains at five cell heights and tests each model at three. These results demonstrate that: 1) accuracy is insensitive to the cell height itself, as the three matched settings from 48 to 80 pixels lie within 0.8 ACC points in English (85.08, 85.89, 85.44) and 0.5 in Chinese (75.53, 76.00, 75.72), so 48-pixel atlas, 44% smaller than 64-pixel one, costs under one point; 2) English is insensitive to traintest mismatch as well, staying within 82.7786.25 over the whole grid, since Latin strokes remain several latent pixels wide even at 48 pixels; 3) Chinese is sensitive to mismatch, and the drop grows with the gap and is steepest when testing below the training height, from 75.72 to 60.95 for model trained at 80 pixels and tested at 48, and from 75.33 to 48.18 for one trained at 96, as the strokes of complex characters no longer appear at the density the model learned to read them. Cell resolution can therefore be chosen by budget, provided the model has seen the chosen heights during training, which is why the random resolution augmentation of Sec. 3.3 of the main paper draws from 48, 64, and 80 pixels, the range over which matched accuracy is flat. Under the allocator the longest atlas shrinks from 784 to 512 tokens in English and from 1,200 to 794 in Chinese, while the mean changes by under 11% because the allocator also raises the cells of short atlases: its role is to bound the sequence length of text-heavy scenes, not to cut the average cost. Inference cost. The atlas appends tokens to the two scenesized streams, which already carry 1,024 tokens each, so the mean atlas length of 291 English and 175 Chinese tokens at 64 pixels is small fraction of the sequence. Measured on A800-80GB GPUs at 512 512 with 10 Euler steps, generation takes on average 5.18s per English and 4.30s per Chinese image at 64 pixels, with per-process peak of about 32.1 GiB, dominated by the resident model. Lowering to 48 pixels cuts the atlas by 44% and shortens generation by about 3%, and the allocator controls the long tail without measurable change in mean runtime. The extra cost over glyph-image-only conditioning is thus the appended atlas tokens, bounded by the allocator and traded against stroke detail through cell resolution.
